title: Compromise Infrastructure: Web Services
summary: Rather than building new infrastructure, the adversary takes over an existing account on a third-party web service such as a code host, social platform, file-sharing site or bulk email provider, and reuses that provider's reputation as a launch point. Because the traffic flows to and from subdomains of well-known services, it blends into the noise defenders already tolerate. Detection depends on account-level telemetry rather than destination reputation: authentication events from unusual locations or user agents, sudden creation of application programming interface keys, outbound mail from a mailbox that normally sends a handful of messages a day, or a repository that starts hosting payloads. The distinguishing signal is a change in behaviour for one identity, since the same domain is used legitimately all day long.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker takes over someone else's account on a well-known website. The website could be a code host, a social network, a file store or an email sending service. The attacker does not build anything new. Instead, they hide their work inside a service that people already trust.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies block unknown websites but allow popular ones. When an attacker sends commands or stolen files through a trusted service, that traffic looks normal. Your users may also trust a message that comes from a familiar domain. If you ignore account activity, a stolen login can sit quietly for weeks. Spotting the takeover early is often the only chance to stop the next stage.
howItWorks: The attacker gets login details for a real user account, often through phishing or a reused password.
They sign in and change the recovery settings so the real owner cannot easily take the account back.
They create application keys that let scripts use the service without needing a password each time.
The account then hosts malicious files, sends phishing email or relays stolen data onward.
Legitimate users keep using the same service, so the provider domain itself looks harmless.
Defenders notice the change by comparing the account's normal behaviour with its new activity.
beginner.example: Think of a shared office building with one main entrance. Everyone trusts the building because the reception desk is well known and the doors are locked. An attacker does not break the door. They steal a tenant's key card and then walk in and out all day. The guard sees the same corridor, the same lift and the same badge reader. Nothing looks strange until someone checks that this tenant used to leave at six and now visits the storage room at midnight. The building is not the problem. The stolen key is.
takeaways: A trusted website is only as safe as the accounts that people use on it.
Watch for sudden changes in one account, not just for unknown domain names.
Turn on multi-factor authentication so a stolen password is not enough on its own.

objectives: Explain how a compromised web service account can be abused for command and control or phishing.
Identify the account and application key telemetry that reveals a takeover on a third-party service.
Distinguish malicious use of a popular service from ordinary business traffic.
Describe why reputation-based blocking alone fails against this technique.
List the hardening steps that reduce the value of a stolen service account.
